The record is correctly constructed: it satisfies every rule the Evaluation Process Ontology's shapes state about how an evaluation must be recorded. A mechanical yes or no, produced by machine. Rulings R-31 and R-32: the steps are not invented. Each step in vocabulary/epo.ttl cites the process step it matches: the contracting lifecycle (need, propose, agree, access, deliver, accept) matches the ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 agreement processes, ISO/IEC 17000 access, scheme and acceptance, ISO 9000 contract and the 29119-2 test environment and completion report; scope and declare requirements match the ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 acquisition, stakeholder needs definition and system requirements definition processes as SEBoK describes them; plan, execute and report match the ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-2 test strategy and planning, test execution and test completion processes as SEVOCAB defines them; determine and attest matches ISO/IEC 17000's review, decision and attestation. The EPO operationalizes those steps as executable checks.

The reusable, domain-independent description of how a rigorous evaluation is run: the standard operating procedure whose six steps, performed inside the contracting lifecycle, make a coverage claim checkable when followed. It assumes a Domain-Specific Ontology is in place and does not change across domains.

Ruling R-17. Downward: requirement to acceptance criteria to test plan to probes (shapes S2, S3). Upward: attestation to evidence to turn to probe to criterion to requirement (shapes S6, S8; queries/traceback.rq). Coverage: the weighted share of criteria with an attested outcome (shape S7; queries/coverage.rq).

The record of one evaluation, bound by the Evaluation Process Ontology: the DSO release, the requirement set, the test plan, the probes, the sessions and their trajectories, the evidence, the attestations, the report and the recommendations, with who did what and when. The EPO determines what must be present for requirements traceability in both directions and for coverage, and makes all three checkable by machine; a conformant record therefore provides both traceability directions and coverage.

A system that, given the same inputs and starting state, will not always produce the same outputs. The system under test is one, which is why a single probe is weak evidence and why pass rates are estimated over replicate sessions.
epo:Evidence (bears on one criterion, under a test plan) derived from epo:Response or epo:Trajectory
Rulings R-18 and R-20: evidence exists at probe, session or suite level and maps to an expected result; it is the domain, and the determination on it is the codomain.

Data that supports the existence or truth of something. Here, what is collected as the basis for a determination: a response at one turn, a session's trajectory, or several of them rolled up over a test suite, as in a robustness battery. Each evidence item bears on one acceptance criterion's expected result and is bound to the test plan it was collected under. Evidence is the domain; the determination made on it, passed, failed or cannot tell, is the codomain. On its own evidence verifies nothing; a determination rules on it and an attestation judges it.

Contextual AI Evaluation performed with the method this specification sets out: the Evaluation Process Ontology, the same six steps for every domain inside a contracting lifecycle, applied with a Domain-Specific Ontology supplied or approved by the domain's experts, leaving a record anyone can check for conformance, traceability and coverage.
A shared, formal vocabulary for a domain, precise enough that a computer can check whether a body of data follows its rules.
epo:RequirementSet with epo:environment and epo:systemUnderTest; sysml item def RequirementSet

Rulings R-03 and R-14: a house label for the requirement set bound to one system under test in one operational environment; not a coinage. Two evaluations are comparable only when they share an envelope.

The requirements this system under test must meet in this operational environment, with their acceptance criteria and weights, declared before any probe is run. It refines the idea of a requirement by adding specificity: the same system in a different environment, or a different system in the same environment, gets a different envelope. That is what makes the evaluation contextual, and what separates it from a benchmark; the nearest practice is that of safety-critical systems. Coverage is measured over the envelope and only over it.

The conditions and assumptions about the deployment setting under which acceptable behavior is defined: who uses the system, for what, and what is out of scope.

A person or group of people with its own functions, responsibilities and authorities. Three organizations are parties to every OG-CAIE evaluation: the sponsor organization that commissions it, the testing organization that performs it, and the organization accountable for the test item. The result recorded for a judgment: passed, failed, cannot tell, inapplicable, or untested. Not binary on purpose.
A measurable result. Here: how the system did on what was exercised, reported as the pass, fail and cannot-tell fractions of the covered criteria. Never merged with coverage.

A scenario tied to the acceptance criteria it exercises, derived from the Domain-Specific Ontology and checked for consistency before use, applied at one turn of a session. Ruling R-21: the testing organization. ISO 9000:2026 3.1.9 Note 2 says a provider in a contractual situation is sometimes called a contractor, hence the altLabel.

The organization that provides the evaluation as a service: the testing organization. Its account executive signs the contract, its evaluation team does the work, and its machines keep the record. Independent of the accountable organization, its activity is second-party when a sponsor with a user interest commissions it (ISO/IEC 17000 4.4, Note 2) and third-party when no interested party does.
A document stating results achieved or giving evidence of activities performed. The evaluation record is the record of one evaluation.

How closely results agree when the same measurement is repeated under the same conditions: same system version, same procedure, same operator or policy, same session protocol, over a short period. Replicate sessions under repeatability conditions are what turn a probe into a pass rate.
the record's fixed frame: requirement set, DSO release, test plan, session protocol

How closely results agree when the measurement is repeated under changed conditions: different operators, different sessions, a different evaluation team. Two evaluations that share a requirement set and a DSO release are comparable to the extent their results reproduce.
Something the system must do, or a condition it must meet, to be fit for its purpose. Broad requirements are decomposed into acceptance criteria that can be checked one at a time.
the chain requirement, acceptance criterion, test plan, probe, turn, evidence, attestation in the record; queries/traceback.rq

Ruling R-15: requirements traceability and metrological traceability are kept distinct, but they are in principle the same idea at different levels of abstraction once both are done computationally over knowledge graphs. Here computational instruments measure computational systems, so the metrological sense still applies: the chain from a reported number back to the record is an unbroken documented chain, and the pass rate it reaches carries a measurement uncertainty.
The documented path linking what was required to how it was tested and what was found, so a coverage claim can be checked by anyone holding the record.
Testing in which what is tested, and how much, is chosen according to analyzed risk. Deployment sensitivity is the weight that makes coverage reflect consequence.
A step-by-step description of a situation the system is put through: the user, their circumstances, and what they ask. A scenario becomes a probe once it is tied to the criteria it exercises.

One pairing of one tester with one system under test, in which a sequence of turns is run. Sessions are stateful: what the system says at a later turn depends on everything said before, so evidence belongs to its session, not only to its probe.

The expert judgment that the evidence gathered is enough to support the claim being made. A quantity judgment, distinct from appropriateness. A judgment with no evidence cannot record a pass or a fail.

Ruling R-10: the ISO entry is marked <audit>; here the team is an evaluation team, not an audit team, and both the domain expert and the evaluation operator are technical experts on it (R-23 names the second). Assessors of the assessment are out of scope (R-11).

A person who provides specific knowledge or expertise to the evaluation team. Two kinds sit on the team. The domain expert is expert in the Domain-Specific Ontology: they supply or approve its release, attest that it is appropriate for the case being evaluated (this system under test, these requirements, this operational environment), and may be consulted on interpreting evidence. The evaluation operator is expert in performing the tests the Evaluation Process Ontology specifies, conditioned on the DSO, and in assembling the evidence.
epo:Session with its epo:Turn activities (test execution; each turn's epo:Response is the actual result)

Finding out whether requirements for a specific intended use are met. A session, in which probes are run turn by turn against the system under test, is a test; the evidence its turns yield feeds the attestations.
Inputs, execution conditions and expected results developed for a particular objective. The abstract test; a probe is a test case tied to the criteria it exercises.

Ruling R-01: coverage relates requirements to the abstract tests that cover them. The acceptance criterion is the coverage item and the probe is the test case; the concrete applications of a probe during a case produce evidence, which is rolled up by attestation. Coverage counts criteria with an attested outcome; it does not count evidence.
How much of the declared acceptance criteria the evaluation actually reached, as a share weighted by deployment sensitivity. It says how much was evaluated, not how well the system did.
sysml part def TestItem; earl:TestSubject and prov:SoftwareAgent; epo:systemUnderTest on the requirement set

Ruling R-19: the only standard definition of the phrase system under test is a 1999 performance-measurement one (ISO/IEC 14756), so the headword is test item (29119-2), from the same family as test case, test plan and test strategy; the systems-engineering reading is system-of-interest (15288) and the AI-evaluation reading is NIST's application. The phrase system under test stays in prose and in the model as the alternative label.
The deployed AI system being evaluated, taken as a black box: only what it is given and what it produces are recorded. The prose calls it the system under test; the standard headword is test item.
epo:TestPlan, a prov:Entity; sysml item def TestPlan

The statement, made before any test runs, of what the evaluation will test and how: which acceptance criteria are its objectives, which probes are its means, and what each probe is expected to show. Derived from the requirement set and the Domain-Specific Ontology in step three; every attestation is bound to the plan that produced its evidence.
epo:Strategy, a prov:Plan; a TestPlan's means alongside listed probes

Ruling R-13: anchored to output feedback because the record only ever holds outputs; the memory operator with the DSO as model is the observer. Semantic state feedback is the authors' framing, kept as an alternative label.

The part of a test plan that decides which probe comes next from the trajectory so far, grounded in the Domain-Specific Ontology, rather than listing probes in advance. It closes a loop: the system's outputs feed back into the choice of the next input. A human red teamer following their own judgment is one such strategy; a written policy is another.
epo:TestSuite, a prov:Activity grouping epo:Session activities

A set of sessions run together, for example replicate sessions of one strategy, or the varied sessions of a sensitivity test or robustness battery. Evidence rolled up over a suite is evidence at the third level, above probe and session.
epo:independentOfAccountable on the testing organization (record fact, S0)

Evaluation performed by an organization independent of the provider of the test item and with no user interest in it, and not on behalf of anyone who has one. Independence of the testing organization from the accountable organization is what makes an OG-CAIE result independent; the record states it as a fact about the parties rather than assuming it, and states separately whether the sponsor has a user interest.
epo:Trajectory, a prov:Entity generated by a Session; ordered epo:Turn activities
Ruling R-13: the IEC trajectory runs through the hidden state x; what the record holds is the input-output realization, which specializes it to what is observable.

The recorded sequence of prompt and response pairs of a session, in order. The system's internal state is never observed; the trajectory is the observable realization, and plays the role a time series of measurements plays in system identification. A small change early in a trajectory can change everything after it.

Confirming with objective evidence that the requirements for a specific intended use were fulfilled. Applied to the evaluation itself: was it aimed at the right problem and is the evidence enough. Both are human judgments, recorded in the attestation.
SHACL shapes S1-S8 (machine); SCI requirements tagged machine

Confirming with objective evidence that specified requirements were fulfilled. Applied to the evaluation itself: did it exercise what it declared, and was its declared process followed. Both are mechanical checks over the record.
The Domain-Specific Ontology release is versioned and approved by a named domain expert before any probe is derived from it.
The service agreement, the operational environment, the test item and the requirement set are declared, in that order, before any session runs: this system in this environment under this contract.
Every requirement has at least one acceptance criterion derived from it; every criterion states its expected result and carries a positive weight.
A test plan states its objectives and its means; every probe belongs to a plan, derives from the DSO release and passes a consistency check before any session.
Every response comes from a numbered turn of a session against a versioned test item; every evidence item bears on one criterion's expected result under the plan.
machine for form; human for the judgment

Determinations rule on evidence with an EARL outcome; attestations aggregate a criterion's determinations, name their assertor, and judge appropriateness and sufficiency; the closure and chain rules hold.
Coverage is recomputable from a conformant record: a criterion counts as covered only with an attestation behind it.
Coverage and performance are reported together and never merged.
machine for the trace; human for the recommendation
Every recommendation traces to the attestations it rests on, their evidence, the DSO release and the EPO step.

The sponsor, the testing organization and the accountable organization are named; the sponsor's mission and obligations towards the affected populations are recorded before the need, and its statement of work decides, per population, interview or representation; the agreement is signed by the sponsor and the account executive; every affected population is interviewed or represented by a named domain expert.

The wiring guarantees the end state, checked locally over kinds of parts and ports: every wire runs from an output port on a part to an input port on a part carrying one item kind; at every part every input is present once and every output goes somewhere; every item kind reaches the recorder; the seven steps form a process DAG that produces every item kind; a conformant record then yields traceability in both directions and coverage, and answers why.

The domain expert who approves the DSO, assesses appropriateness and attests is not the evaluation operator who administers tests and collects evidence, and neither is the account executive who signs the agreement; one account executive, one or more of each expert.

What the contract pins (the counterparties, the test item, the requirements' frame, the method) is recorded and closed before what the evaluation pins (the environment, the requirement set, the DSO release, the plan) is declared; the evaluation documents the first layer and cannot change it.

nodes.desc: Targets sysml:PartDefinition. The assembly relates the sponsor to the affected populations by an obligation: a connection usage typed Obligation whose ends are the sponsor part and the affected part, a relation that carries no item (R-38). nodes.label: M1-Obligation

nodes.desc: Targets sysml:PartDefinition. The assembly owns a part typed AffectedPopulation with lower bound zero: populations are many and may be absent (R-21). The assembly owns exactly one part typed by each of SponsorOrganization, TestingOrganization and AccountableOrganization (R-21).
nodes.label: M1-Parties

nodes.desc: Targets sysml:PartDefinition. At the part: every input port is present on exactly one wire (input wires are unique, R-25, R-26). At the part: every output port goes somewhere, on one wire or several, since what flows is information (R-25, R-26).
nodes.label: M2-Part

nodes.desc: Targets sysml:InterfaceUsage. A wire runs from an output port on a part to an input port on a part: the output end is a plain port owned by a part definition, the input end a conjugated one (R-26). The input port's type is the wire's consumer end type, conjugated: it receives the same item kind. The output port's type is the wire's supplier end type: what flows is one item kind. A wire comes from exactly one output port. A wire goes to exactly one input port.
nodes.label: M2-Wire

nodes.desc: Targets sysml:PortDefinition. Every item kind that crosses a seam reaches the recorder: the recorder owns a conjugated port of this type (R-17).
nodes.label: M3-RecordHub

nodes.desc: Targets sysml:ItemDefinition. Every item kind is an out parameter of some step of the process, or the process's own result: nothing in the record appears from nowhere.
nodes.label: M4-EveryItemProduced

nodes.desc: Targets sysml:ActionDefinition. One nested model (R-33): the contracting lifecycle's fulfil step is a black box typed by the evaluation process. The inner process conforms to the layer above: every input of the evaluation process is fed by a flow from a contracting step, and every output feeds one (R-33).
nodes.label: M4-Nesting

nodes.desc: Targets sysml:SuccessionAsUsage. The EPO is a process DAG (R-26): no step succeeds itself, directly or through other steps.
nodes.label: M4-ProcessDag

nodes.desc: Targets sysml:ActionDefinition. The evaluation owns exactly six steps; the contracting lifecycle owns six of its own plus the nested fulfil step (R-21, R-32, R-33). The steps succeed one another in the fixed order: scope, declareRequirements, plan, execute, determineAndAttest, report for the evaluation; need, propose, agree, access, fulfil, deliver, acceptDelivery for the contracting lifecycle.

nodes.desc: Targets sysml:PartDefinition. The evaluation team allows one or more domain experts and one or more operators: lower bound one, upper bound unbounded (R-23). The testing organization holds exactly one account executive (R-23).

nodes.desc: Targets sysml:PortUsage. DSO, appropriateness assessment, plan approval and attestation are supplied only by the domain expert (R-10, R-21). nodes.desc: Targets sysml:Package. The testing organization holds an account executive and a team of at least one domain expert and one evaluation operator. The three actor categories are distinct part definitions of Person: DomainExpert, EvaluationOperator, AccountExecutive (R-10, R-23).

nodes.desc: test coverage: abstract tests vs concrete applications (H, ruled). The paper draft conflates tests (abstract) that cover requirements with the concrete applications of those tests during a case, which produce the evidence. Z's comment on the draft (2026-09-05): "it seems to conflate tests (abstract) with (concrete) applications of those tests ... test coverage ... relates the requirements we carry about to tests (abstract) that cover them; Not the specific incidents (plural) of those tests applied during a specific case. the latter produces the evidence which is ultimately rolled up to support validating (or invalidating) the hypothesis that the requirement is met." SEVOCAB carries ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-2:2021 3.28 test coverage, which supports the abstract reading.
nodes.label: C-01

nodes.desc: operating environment: which canonical anchor (M, ruled). Term contract v5 anchors "operating environment" to the automotive Operational Design Domain (SAE J3016, SAE J3259, ISO 34503), all paid sources outside the evaluation domain. SEVOCAB carries "operational environment" (IEEE 982-2024 3.1): physical context, setting, and circumstances used to support the in-service operation of a system.
nodes.label: C-02

nodes.desc: operational envelope: no canonical entry (M, ruled). Neither ISO 9000:2026 nor SEVOCAB defines "operational envelope". Term contract v5 cites process-safety usage (CCPS "safe operating envelope"), a weak fit. Functionally the envelope is the declared requirement set with its acceptance criteria and weights for the operational environment.
nodes.label: C-03

nodes.desc: redistribution of source snapshots (M, ruled). SEBoK v2.14 is CC BY-NC-SA; the ISO 9000:2026 OBP preview is copyrighted text captured as 37 screenshots. Committing either to a public repository is a licence exposure; not committing them weakens machine verification of quotes in CI.
nodes.label: C-04

nodes.desc: deployment sensitivity: refined term or coinage (L, ruled). The weight on each acceptance criterion by consequence of failure. SEVOCAB carries risk-based testing (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-2:2021 3.16). Is "deployment sensitivity" a refinement of that or a fourth coinage.
nodes.label: C-05

nodes.desc: IRI base: w3id now or Pages URL (L, ruled). Ontology and record IRIs need a stable base. w3id.org/og-caie requires a PR to perma-id/w3id.org and resolves nowhere until merged; the GitHub Pages URL resolves immediately but renaming later breaks every Turtle file.
nodes.label: C-06

nodes.desc: scope: requirements and interfaces, or architecture too (M, ruled). Z's SEBoK screenshots draw the scope box around Concept Definition and System Requirements Definition (including Assess Interactions across Interfaces) and stop before Logical and Physical Architecture. The infra drawing (frontend, backend, data) is a realization sketch. Do part and port defs stay at the interface level or allocate to that drawing.
nodes.label: C-07

nodes.desc: adequacy vs appropriateness (H, ruled). The paper draft and term contract v5 label the attestation's context judgment "adequacy". The primary source for the pairing (Hawkins, Kelly, Knight and Graydon 2011, assurance claim points) uses "appropriateness" for asserted context and "sufficiency" for asserted solution; ISA 500 uses appropriateness (quality) and sufficiency (quantity). "Adequacy" also collides with ISO 9000:2026 3.11.2 review.
nodes.label: C-08

nodes.desc: the coinage set: which terms do we own (H, ruled). Term contract v5 tags probe/scenario, deployment sensitivity, DSO, EPO and CAIE as [CAIE] assemblies. Under the rule that terms are used, not owned, which of these are coinages the project must own, and which are refinements of standard terms.
nodes.label: C-09

nodes.desc: system under test: weak canonical entry (L, ruled). SEVOCAB's only entry for "system under test (SUT)" reads "parts of the CBSS to be tested" (ISO/IEC 14756:1999, a performance-measurement standard). The cleaner entries are "test item: work product to be tested" (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-2:2021) and "system-of-interest: system whose life cycle is under consideration" (ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2026). The paper says "system under test" throughout. Options: keep SUT as prefLabel with the weak quote (current), or make "test item" canonical with SUT as altLabel.
nodes.label: C-10

nodes.desc: technical expert: one kind or several on the evaluation team (M, ruled). ISO 9000:2026 3.12.9 defines technical expert in the audit context as a person who provides specific knowledge or expertise to the audit team. The glossary had bound it only to the DomainExpert part. Who else on the evaluation team is a technical expert, and in what.
nodes.label: C-11

nodes.desc: assessing the assessors (L, ruled). Technical experts may in principle have mirrored counterparts who assess the assessment (second-party review, as in the June prototype's audit module). Does this specification model them.
nodes.label: C-12

nodes.desc: the chain from requirement to attestation: is the test plan explicit (H, ruled). The record linked requirement to criterion, probe to criterion, run to probe, evidence to run, and attestation to criterion and evidence. It had no test plan node, no expected result on the criterion, and no binding from the attestation to the probe whose run produced its evidence, so the interpretation was not mechanically tied to the plan that produced what it interpreted.
nodes.label: C-13

nodes.desc: probe versus run: trajectories, sessions and state feedback policies (H, ruled). The record has one probe, one run and one evidence, which hides a distinction Z draws: a probe is an individual prompt-response pair; a run is a sequence of prompt-response pairs forming a trajectory within a session; sessions are stateful and LLM-system behaviour is highly context sensitive, nonlinear in the sense that a small change in input can cause large changes in output, especially when trajectories are continued. Test plans are not limited to single probes: they support strategies that determine probes according to a state feedback policy (semantic state feedback). Z: this is the place where a small amount of extra definition drawn from control engineering, system identification and metrology as applied to dynamical systems has the most to gain; hunt for canonical sources, starting with NIST.
nodes.label: C-14

nodes.desc: operational envelope: what it adds to a set of requirements (M, ruled). R-03 kept operational envelope as a house label anchored to ISO 9000:2026 requirement. Is it merely the set of requirements, or does it carry more: the binding of those requirements to one system under test in one operational environment.
nodes.label: C-15

nodes.desc: requirements traceability and metrological traceability (M, ruled). ISO 9000:2026 3.5.11 Note 2 defers the metrological sense of traceability to ISO/IEC Guide 99 (the VIM). The glossary anchored requirements traceability to 29148 via SEVOCAB and kept metrology out. Should the metrological sense be visible, and how do the two relate.
nodes.label: C-16

nodes.desc: conformity, conformance, and what SHACL calls validation (H, ruled). ISO 9000:2026 3.5.9 deprecates conformance as a synonym of conformity. W3C SHACL calls its machine check validation, which by this specification's V and V split is verification. The glossary had one term, conformity, and banned conformance. How to name the machine-checked, correctly constructed record without confusing it with fulfilment of a requirement in the ISO sense, or with validation.
nodes.label: C-17

nodes.desc: evaluation record: what the EPO binds it to provide (M, ruled). Is the evaluation record merely a record in the ISO sense, or is it bound by the EPO to contain what traceability and coverage need, and is that binding checkable.
nodes.label: C-18

nodes.desc: evidence: at what level, and what it maps to (H, ruled). The record bound each evidence item to one turn's response and the attestation to the probe. Evidence can also exist at the session level (a trajectory) and rolled up over many sessions (a sensitivity test or robustness battery), so binding to a probe is too narrow; and nothing said what an evidence item is evidence of.
nodes.label: C-19

nodes.desc: evidence and determination: domain and codomain (H, ruled). R-18 was implemented with the determination folded into the evidence item as a Boolean observed value. Z, rereading: that is wrong; evidence is the domain and the determination is the codomain, and the determination is not strictly Boolean because EARL admits cantTell.
nodes.label: C-20

nodes.desc: parties to the evaluation are implicit (H, ruled). The model and record name persons on an evaluation team and a system under test but no organizations: nobody sponsors the evaluation, nobody is accountable for the test item, nobody performs the testing as a service, and the affected stakeholders have no place. The wiring cannot guarantee an end state it does not know the parties to.
nodes.label: C-21

nodes.desc: which artifact is canonical: the SysML source or its RDF rendering (H, ruled). OpenSysML v0.4.3 cannot quantify over collections, so value-level guarantees cannot be written as SysML constraints; and the model's `-convert ttl` rendering is deterministic, uses the OMG SysML vocabulary with stable element IRIs, and is the form Flexo MMS ingests. The question was whether the SysML text or the rendered graph is the canonical structure, and what the SysML is for.
nodes.label: C-22

nodes.desc: actor categories on the testing organization's side, and named persons in the demo (M, ruled). The plan carried two human roles (domain expert, evaluator) and no signatory for the service agreement; and the worked example used anonymous role-holders (an epidemiologist, a community educator, a red-teamer).
nodes.label: C-23

nodes.desc: contract: no capture of ISO 9000:2026 clause 3.3.13 (L, ruled). The 37 screenshots skip clauses 3.3.9 to 3.3.15, so the 2026 wording of contract is not held. The glossary entry carries the 2015 wording (3.4.7, "binding agreement") as a pending quote naming the screenshot still to be captured (iso-9000-2026-obp-38). Z: capture 3.3.9 to 3.3.15 and tick sheet 03 row 7.
nodes.label: C-24

nodes.desc: first, second and third party: three adopted terms or one refined term (L, open). ISO/IEC 17000 defines first-, second- and third-party conformity assessment activity as three headwords. The glossary adopts all three verbatim (no coinage); the alternative is one refined term, conformity assessment party, with the three as altLabels, which would be a fourth coinage. Z to confirm the three-term reading or rule otherwise.
nodes.label: C-25

nodes.desc: account executive: canonical anchor (L, open). No ranked source defines account executive. The entry is anchored, provisionally, as a specialization of ISO 9000:2026 3.1.3 top management (the person top management authorizes to sign for the organization); ISO/IEC 17000 4.3 Note 1 (parties to a contract) and 4.6 conformity assessment body are the alternatives. Z to confirm or redirect.
nodes.label: C-26

nodes.desc: port reuse across actor categories: activities confused with actors (M, ruled). The first structure-only model let the account executive deliver the report and the recommendation through ports typed by the operator's RecommendationWrite and the calculator's ReportWrite, and the wiring test excused the reuse as by design. Delivering is a different activity from recommending, with its own output.
nodes.label: C-27

nodes.desc: one wire per port, or shared output wires (M, ruled). The first wiring rule required every port to be the end of exactly one seam, which forced the recorder to carry six identical record outputs, the probe deriver two probe outputs and the account executive two delivery outputs, one per reader.
nodes.label: C-28

nodes.desc: what the wiring rules are rules over, and what the EPO is as a process (M, ruled). The first M-shapes were a mixed bag: some per port, some per interface, one over the package. Z asked for rules that can be checked and explained locally, defined over kinds of parts and kinds of ports; and for the EPO to be read as a process DAG, with loops admitted only if the end state needs them.
nodes.label: C-29

nodes.desc: the revised model is a draft: block-by-block validation and the end-state demonstration are still to come (H, open). Z, on tagging v0.2.0: "i still need to work through the model step by step and validate all the individual blocks and wires. and need to make sure we get a computational demonstration of our epo guaranteeing a complete record with full traceability and coverage. that is still work to come." The M-shapes check that the wiring is well formed; nothing yet shows that every run of the process must yield a record conforming to S0 to S8.
nodes.label: C-30

nodes.desc: evaluation team anchored to audit team: the word audit reads as legal (M, ruled). Z, reviewing sheet 03 row 8: "the word audit feels out of place. most people think of audits and evals differently, as an audit is expected to have legal bearing." The refined term evaluation team is anchored to ISO 9000:2026 3.12.7 audit team ("one or more persons conducting an audit, supported if needed by technical experts"), and technical expert (R-10) to 3.12.9, also marked <audit>. ISO's own definition of audit carries no legal bearing, but readers bring the connotation. Candidate re-anchors: SEVOCAB assessment team, "one or more individuals who jointly perform a process assessment" (ISO/IEC 33001:2015, 3.2.10, p. 30), with audit team as seeAlso; or keep the ISO anchor with a scope note that disclaims the legal reading.
nodes.label: C-31

nodes.desc: the front matter does not prepare the audience; the glossary is rendered whole; Popper is everywhere (H, ruled). Reading the site after v0.2.0, Z found the front page carried the whole vocabulary discipline, the site map and the offers; the glossary page rendered all 58 terms as one table; the Popperian framing was mixed into the technical pages; and there was no shorthand for the class of evaluation the method is for. The audience is not prepared for the contracting workflow and then the evaluation workflow.
nodes.label: C-32

nodes.desc: the bookends test banned ordinary words (L, ruled). The slice-A test confined hypothesis, prediction, auxiliary, evidence and the like to the front page and the conclusion by word, although they are common English; the restriction Z intended is on using them in Popper's sense with Popper's definitions.
nodes.label: C-33

nodes.desc: the seven steps were not bound to a citation (M, ruled). The EPO's seven steps carried labels and rulings but no citation to a documented process model, although the quality-management and systems-engineering canon documents evaluation processes. Without the binding the steps read as invented rather than operationalized.
nodes.label: C-34

nodes.desc: the contracting lifecycle was absent from the model; the two layers of assumptions were not distinguished (H, ruled). Work on an evaluation is contracted before it is performed, and delivered and accepted after, but the model held only the evaluation, with the agreement as its first step. The contract pins the first layer of auxiliary assumptions (the counterparties, the object, the requirements' frame, the method); the evaluation pins the second. The record did not say which was which.
nodes.label: C-35

nodes.desc: two cycles as two action defs, or one nested model (M, ruled). After R-32 the assembly performed two actions side by side, the contracting lifecycle and the evaluation, with the handoff stated only in prose. SysML can nest: an action usage typed by another action def is a black box with defined inputs and outputs, and that action def is its drill-down, conforming to the interface above by typing. Z asked whether OpenSysML gives us that power and, if so, to make it the way the two layers are modeled.
nodes.label: C-36

nodes.desc: the site had no stated relation to the model; pages were not paired specification and example (H, ruled). The site grew page by page without a stated principle of what each page is a view of, and its pages did not pair the abstract specification with the concrete example. Z replanned it as a presentation layer over a self-documenting model.
nodes.label: C-37

nodes.desc: what happens after acceptance: narration, not a step (L, ruled). The contracting walkthrough ended at acceptance. In practice the sponsor tells the accountable organization to change the system per the findings, the change is made, and the sponsor may require new testing to certify it. Whether to model that or narrate it was open.
nodes.label: C-38

nodes.desc: surveillance as a headword raises eyebrows (L, ruled). R-35 quoted ISO/IEC 17000 8.1 surveillance in the Contracting walkthrough. The clause is the formal doctrine for a repeat evaluation and must stay mapped, but the word reads badly to a general audience.
nodes.label: C-39

nodes.desc: no seam carried the sponsor's obligations towards the affected populations (M, ruled). The contracting slice of the wiring carried the need, the proposal, the agreement, the access, the delivery and the acceptance, but nothing about what the sponsor owes the affected populations: its expressed mission, duties and obligations, which is the context the contract answers to.
nodes.label: C-40

nodes.desc: the mission's relation to the affected populations was in the record but not in the model or the view (M, ruled). The record said which populations the sponsor's mission regards, but the SysML model held no relation between the sponsor and the affected populations, and the contracting wiring diagram drew none. Diagrams were also growing dense: one edge per seam, named by the seam, with no statement of what the view brings into focus or leaves out.
nodes.label: C-41

nodes.desc: every chapter says there is more in the model, but a human reader has only the files and the CLI to find it (L, ruled). The site curates; block 5 of every chapter points to the repository and to ogc. A human reader without a shell has no interface to the model behind the pages, and the prose grows to compensate.
nodes.label: C-42

nodes.desc: the S-shapes judge the items that exist; no shape requires a step's output to exist (M, open). The executor's mutations show that a record without a plan approval, or without an access grant, conforms to S0 to S9: the shapes constrain a plan approval or an access grant once present but do not require one. Completeness against the model catches both, and the missing access also empties the traceback. Question for Z: should the S-shapes require the existence of each step's outputs (a test plan approved by a domain expert before any session; an access grant behind every session), or is completeness against the model the right place for existence, keeping the shapes local to the items?
nodes.label: C-43

nodes.desc: ogc has no reader for the record: explorer nodes for record items point at their class, not the item (L, open). The knowledge graph explorer names, on every node, the ogc command that prints it. For record items (track/measles-run.ttl) there is none: the record is not among the files ogc loads, so the node points at a DESCRIBE of the item's class. A --record flag on ogc sparql, or a reader of the record, would close this.
nodes.label: C-44

nodes.desc: the model counterexample no-obligation also fires M5-Cardinality (L, open). counterexamples/model/no-obligation.sysml is built to fail M1-Obligation and does, but its bare testing organization declares no account executive, so M5-Cardinality fires too; the test only asks that the named shape is among those fired. Either the counterexample gains an account executive so that it fails M1-Obligation alone, or the claim is read as sufficiency.
nodes.label: C-45

nodes.desc: the sponsor's decision to interview or represent each affected population had no item of its own (M, ruled). The record showed one population interviewed and one represented, and S0-Population accepted either, but nothing said who decided which, or that the decision was a scope-of-work judgment made with the contract; the evaluation's scope step had no input carrying it.
nodes.label: C-46

nodes.desc: the rulings sat among the chapters as a page most readers will not want (L, ruled). The rulings page was the seventh page of the main path. It is an important record, but it interrupts the arc for a reader who does not need it, and its place in the account of the method (the subjective choices behind the objective results) was not stated.
nodes.label: C-47

nodes.desc: the outline's page names did not tell a skimming reader what the site contains (L, ruled). Glossary, Contracting, The evaluation, What the record proves: each named a page after its device rather than its subject, so the outline read as a list of parts, not as what a reader would find.
nodes.label: C-48

nodes.desc: the toolchain that makes the specification executable was nowhere reviewed for the reader (M, ruled). The site says it is executable and the gate proves it, but no page tells a reader what the environment is, what is pinned, and how to reproduce the checks; without it the computational paradigm reads as another document.
nodes.label: C-49

nodes.desc: the nested lifecycle page was named for the model and did not say that the record rests on both cycles (L, ruled). The page was titled The nested model; and though the record hub receives items from the contracting lifecycle and from the evaluation, the page did not state that the records and the reporting rely on information produced during both.
nodes.label: C-50

nodes.desc: the toolchain review did not say why OpenSysML is outside the runtime environment, nor which ontologies the graphs are written in (L, ruled). Appendix D listed the Python environment, the pinned converter and the vendored libraries, but a reader could ask why OpenSysML is not a dependency of the environment, and nothing reviewed the vocabularies the graphs use: PROV-O, EARL, SKOS, SHACL, OWL, the OMG SysML vocabulary, and the specification's own namespaces.
nodes.label: C-51

nodes.desc: the layers figure on the nested lifecycle page was illegible (M, ruled). The figure tried to show the two chains, the DSO, the execution assemblage and the interpretation in one drawing, and read as a wall of small boxes; it communicated nothing a reader could hold.
nodes.label: C-52

nodes.desc: round one of the simulated user test: fifteen findings that needed a judgment (rulings sheet 06) (H, ruled). Four sandboxed persona reviewers (a human reader, a machine user of ogc, a reproducibility reviewer, a citation auditor) rated the site and reported findings; the code-level ones were fixed; fifteen needed the adjudicator: the front page's opening, the bridge's source, the chapter blocks, the register of the rulings, terms defined at first use, the canonical source of outcome, the rank of TN 1297, fragment quotes, four stretched step matches, the coined terms' internal citations, Popper uncited, a record reader, executor parameters, thirteen pending quotes, and the alignment of Appendix D with the code.
nodes.label: C-53

nodes.desc: SEVOCAB test coverage (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-2:2021 3.28) is adopted. The distinction between the abstract tests that cover requirements and the concrete applications of those tests during a case, which produce the evidence, is recorded as a scope note rather than as a term.
nodes.label: R-01

nodes.desc: The headword is operational environment, adopted from SEVOCAB (IEEE 982-2024 3.1). Operating environment remains an alternative label; the automotive Operational Design Domain sources (SAE J3016, SAE J3259, ISO 34503) leave the canon.
nodes.label: R-02

nodes.desc: Operational envelope is kept as a house label, defined by composition and anchored to ISO 9000:2026 3.5.1 requirement as a specialization, with requirement set as an alternative label. It is not counted as a coinage.
nodes.label: R-03

nodes.desc: SEBoK v2.14 and the ISO 9000:2026 screenshots are both held locally and not committed. The repository commits their hashes and digests only, and the checks verify the quotes against the digests.
nodes.label: R-04

nodes.desc: Deployment sensitivity is a refined term that specializes SEVOCAB risk-based testing (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-2:2021 3.16). It is not a coinage.
nodes.label: R-05

nodes.desc: IRIs are authored under https://w3id.org/og-caie/ from the start. The GitHub Pages URL is noted as the fallback until the w3id redirect is merged.
nodes.label: R-06

nodes.desc: The scope is requirements and interfaces; architecture is excluded. Part and port definitions stay at the interface level, and the infrastructure drawing is cited as a realization sketch with nothing allocated to it.
nodes.label: R-07

nodes.desc: The pairing is appropriateness and sufficiency. The earlier label adequacy was a misquotation of the primary source; the functional use was correct and only the label was wrong. The primary source is to be checked and cited correctly.
nodes.label: R-08

nodes.desc: Coinage is confined to the project's novel contributions. The two primary coinages are Domain-Specific Ontology and Evaluation Process Ontology; the method is named either CAIE or Ontology-Grounded CAIE, abbreviated OG-CAIE.
nodes.label: R-09

nodes.desc: The world model has more than one kind of technical expert. The domain expert is a technical expert in the domain-specific ontology: a person who can attest to the appropriateness of the Domain-Specific Ontology for the particular case being evaluated, that is, whether this system under test passes these requirements in this operating environment. The red-teamers are also technical experts, though not in the auditing sense: their expertise is in AI evaluation; they perform the tests the EPO specifies, conditioned on the DSO the domain expert supplies, and their job is to assemble and interpret evidence. Domain experts may be called on to consult on the interpretation of the resulting evidence. Both domain experts and AI experts belong on the evaluation team.
nodes.label: R-10

nodes.desc: Technical experts may in principle have mirrored counterparts who assess the assessment, but this document does not model assessing the assessors. The one plausible place for the idea is a closing call to action, offering the reader OG-CAIE or an audit of the reader's own AI evaluation practice against this specification.
nodes.label: R-11

nodes.desc: Traceability from the requirement, as a hypothesis that may be falsified, through an epistemically valid process that collects and interprets evidence to render the judgement, is critical for requirements to be useful concepts. The existing definitions are not to be overwritten. The record must carry a chain of evidence connecting the test plans to the evidence they would produce, the implementation of those plans that produces the evidence, the interpretation of that evidence, and the justified attestation that a requirement is or is not met, bound to that evidence and to the test plan that produced it. This is the level of abstraction at which the abstract EPO is encoded.
nodes.label: R-12

nodes.desc: The eight-term package is adopted as proposed: session and dialogue (NIST); trajectory, with the output-feedback anchor for the policy (IEC 60050-351); test strategy (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-2); non-deterministic system (29119-11); repeatability, reproducibility and measurement uncertainty (VIM, NIST TN 1297). Session and Turn enter the record; a Strategy is a plan's means; the chain rule is extended accordingly.
nodes.label: R-13

nodes.desc: The operational envelope refines the concept of requirements in its specificity: it conditions explicitly on an operating environment and on the system under test, stating that this system in this environment must meet these requirements. It is closely related to a set of requirements, but Contextual AI Evaluation expects different requirements for different systems under test in different operating environments. The distinction is deliberate: it separates the method from benchmarks and aligns it with the practice for safety-critical systems.
nodes.label: R-14

nodes.desc: Requirements traceability and metrological traceability are kept distinct. When both are done computationally with knowledge graphs they can be chained, because they are in principle the same notion at different levels of abstraction. A note records that computational instruments are used to measure computational systems, so the concept of metrological traceability still applies.
nodes.label: R-15

nodes.desc: Since ISO deprecates conformance, the word is reclaimed for the specific requirement that the record be correctly constructed according to the SHACL shapes, and conformity is used for fulfilment of a requirement in the ISO sense. The reclamation is to be noted explicitly. One reason for it is to break the problem that SHACL "validation" is, by this specification's standard, verification; using conformance specifically for the correct-construction requirements applied to the record keeping the EPO demands makes it a special case of conformity that covers requirements which might otherwise create confusion in V&V terms.
nodes.label: R-16

nodes.desc: The evaluation record in this context is bound by the EPO, which determines what must be present for formalized traceability in both directions and for coverage. The EPO makes all three directly checkable by SHACL over the evaluation record; a conformant evaluation record therefore provides both traceability directions and coverage.
nodes.label: R-17

nodes.desc: Evidence can exist at the probe level, at the session level, and rolled up to a multi-session scenario such as a sensitivity test or a robustness battery. It is therefore not necessarily bound to a probe, though it may be. Evidence must be related to the test plan and in particular maps to an expected result: something that can be ruled on directly as a Boolean, whether it did or did not happen.
nodes.label: R-18

nodes.desc: The recommendation on C-10 is accepted, option (b): the headword is test item (SEVOCAB, ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-2:2021, work product to be tested), with system under test, SUT, test object, application and system of interest as alternative labels and the related entries as seeAlso citations. Prose and the model may continue to say system under test.
nodes.label: R-19

nodes.desc: The R-18 implementation is wrong: evidence is the domain and the determination is the codomain. Evidence is collected and serves as the basis for a determination of whether the expected outcome has been met. The determination is not strictly Boolean: per EARL, cantTell is admitted.
nodes.label: R-20

nodes.desc: Explicit stakeholders are introduced. There are affected stakeholders; the organization responsible for the system under test (the test item); the organization performing the testing; and possibly an organization sponsoring the testing that is not the organization operating the test item. Affected stakeholders are populations of actors, whereas the sponsor organization, the testing organization and the organization accountable for the test item are concrete single entities. The requirements are established and agreed between the sponsor organization and the testing organization; the arrangement is viewed as a contract to perform OG-CAIE as a service. The organization that owns the system under test may or may not be the sponsor, and members of the affected stakeholder classes may or may not be interviewed as part of the requirements development process. Most often the interests of affected stakeholders are represented in the requirements on the basis of input from the domain expert, who is employed in the selection of the domain-specific ontology and in the appropriateness assessment of the requirements; the domain expert may also participate in developing or approving test plans, in the interpretation of the evidence collected, and in attestations to the conformity, or not, of the system under test with regard to those requirements under those test plans. This domain expert role is distinct from the expert role responsible for administering the tests and gathering the evidence per the test plan. Part definitions and port definitions specify this as an abstract wiring diagram before it is tested by concrete walkthroughs that exercise the specification on a simple demonstration case.
nodes.label: R-21

nodes.desc: SysML is used primarily for part definitions, port definitions and wiring rules: structure only, with value checks living in SHACL. The rendered RDF version of the models is the canonical record, and the SysML source is treated as a view, even where it is the view used for authoring. OpenSysML renders SysML models as RDF triples because it is designed to work with Flexo MMS; the conversion is deterministic and uses the OMG SysML vocabulary with stable IRIs. A parsimony heuristic prunes the TBox not required by the model, following the pattern applied and described in the authors' earlier work.
nodes.label: R-22

nodes.desc: A domain expert and an evaluation operator are abstract actor categories that populate distinct slots in the EPO. There is also an account executive on the side of the evaluation organization, who is the signatory on the contract and the legal representative of the organization performing the evaluation. The worked example names the Humane Intelligence executive (Mala), the domain expert (Annie) and the evaluation operator (Theo). These are references to real people, but the case is synthetic: the people named will recognise their roles, and they are not asked to make attestations within the demonstration case, which is a simplified synthetic walkthrough of the process. DomainExpert, EvaluationOperator and AccountExecutive are all roles held by members of the company performing the evaluation. Each role must be filled, so there is an at-least-one rule. The account executive is exactly one, being the counterparty who represents the organization in the contract; the domain expert and evaluation operator roles are one or more.
nodes.label: R-23

nodes.desc: Port sharing is bad practice: it confuses activities with actors. Actors may perform multiple activities, but each activity needs precise inputs and outputs.
nodes.label: R-24

nodes.desc: Input wires must be unique. Output wires may be shared, provided that what flows over them is information whose use is nondestructive.
nodes.label: R-25

nodes.desc: Every wiring must be checkable and explainable locally. At the part level, all of a part's input ports and output ports are examined to ensure that every input is present and every output goes somewhere. At the wire level, each wire is examined for where it comes from and where it goes: an output port on a part to an input port on a part. If all rules are defined over kinds of parts and kinds of ports, then enforcing the rules for all parts and wires yields a well-constructed wiring diagram; ports are how wires are addressed. This is essentially the typed block diagram once directionality and the cardinality rules are enforced: one input wire per port, and output wires that may split as long as they are informational. In all likelihood the EPO is a process DAG. Loops are allowed if they are needed to guarantee that the final output record has full requirements traceability in both directions and test coverage, computable by SHACL constraints. The ability to ensure a full record with executable checks on traceability and coverage is precisely what allows the final result to be trusted, and it supports drilling in and deterministically answering the "why" questions related to that result.
nodes.label: R-26

nodes.desc: The ISO 9000:2026 clause for contract is 3.3.13. The page carrying clauses 3.3.9 to 3.3.13 is captured and the quote, binding agreement, is verified; sheet 03 row 7 is ticked.
nodes.label: R-27

nodes.desc: Evaluation team is anchored to the SEVOCAB evaluator. The other two candidates, ISO 9000:2026 3.12.7 audit team and SEVOCAB assessment team (ISO/IEC 33001:2015 3.2.10), are kept as seeAlso citations.
nodes.label: R-28

nodes.desc: The Popper concepts connect to the main OG-CAIE ones through a simple crosswalk table from the Popperian conception of science to the project's terms. The entire glossary is not rendered; the glossary navigation approach from the authors' earlier work is adopted; key terms carry mouse-over definitions in MyST. This plan defers the work through the whole executable EPO specification, with parts, ports and wirings that demonstrably guarantee a scientific record, and the worked health example. The flow for contracting and mapping stakeholders is separated from the flow for performing the evaluation into distinct chapters. All of that remains required, but the glossary is operationalized first and the prose of the first part tightened, so that the audience is prepared to enter the specification for the contracting workflow and then for the evaluation workflow. Each chapter is carefully scoped and revised one at a time as it is reached, working forward. This breaks the modelling into bounded definitions and checks, lowers the modeller's cognitive overhead, and helps present the model clearly in the MyST site. Shorthands are provided: DSO for Domain-Specific Ontology, EPO for Evaluation Process Ontology, CAIE for Contextual AI Evaluation, and OG-CAIE for CAIE performed using the EPO and DSO method this document puts forth. That is the full extent of the coinage; everything else is grounded in cited standards and literature. The Popper-to-standards crosswalk exists to set up what would make the evaluation scientific, and the conclusion must be that OG-CAIE encodes exactly what qualifies as scientific. Popper's definitions occur only in the set-up and in the final conclusion: a coordinate transform from the low-dimensional Popperian conception of science to the high-dimensional engineering standards and back, so that the main narrative arc is accessible to less technical readers. The top-level page is rescoped from why this counts as science onward. The bridge to formal engineering standards for evaluation is the endpoint of the first chapter, which sets up a more rigorous, though not exhaustive, glossary; the glossary in turn supplies the terms needed to express the executable specifications and then to demonstrate their properties.
nodes.label: R-29

nodes.desc: Care is needed with the Popperian terms because they are common English words. The restriction is not on using the words but on using them in Popper's sense with Popper's definitions. The discussion of what is science, grounded in Popper, stays in the bookends, since it is the paper's core argument: "CAIE would be science if it covers these things", ending with "OG-CAIE demonstrably covers these things". The inner sections achieve this through engineering standards. The introduction and conclusion cover why and what; the inner chapters cover what and how in enough detail, and executably, to show both in theory through the executable specification and in practice through the worked example that the bar for science is met.
nodes.label: R-30

nodes.desc: The first page, OG-CAIE as an executable specification, is in good shape for now. One thing stands out: the seven steps are not bound to a citation. Given the INCOSE canon and quality management, a process model for evaluation is almost certainly documented already; it is to be cited and the steps matched to its steps, to reinforce that nothing here is invented, only operationalized through executable code.
nodes.label: R-31

nodes.desc: The contracting lifecycle model receives the same treatment as the evaluation steps. Both cycles are in the paper. The contracting cycle connects to the stakeholders and counterparties and, in this work, pins the first layer of auxiliary assumptions. There must be an explicit separation between the layer of work pinned at the point of the contract and what is pinned and recorded within the scope of an evaluation being performed. Although the evaluation is the main focus, the contract provides axiomatic boundary conditions that bound the scope and also supply assumptions which must be documented for the evaluation to be scientific. The stakeholder terms already introduced are the actors within that lifecycle, which runs from contracting through delivery on the contract. The lifecycle is not to be invented; it is taken from the relevant engineering standards. The contracting lifecycle exists because work has been performed, but it was absent from the model. It is made explicit because it bears on the auxiliary assumptions: the record must distinguish what was pinned by the contract from what was decided in the course of the contract's fulfilment.
nodes.label: R-32

nodes.desc: The two-layer model is to be one model exercising the nesting power of SysML, provided OpenSysML supports it: the outer model treats fulfilment as a black box with well-defined inputs and outputs, and the drill-down specifies that black box in more detail as a specification of its own, which necessarily conforms to the inputs and outputs, and carries the assumptions, of the layer above. This is committed to the plan and to memory as the way the two layers are modelled.
nodes.label: R-33

nodes.desc: The site is replanned. The MyST site is a presentation layer on top of a rich model that documents itself in RDF. The glossary records the terms, their definitions, their lineages, their cross-relationships and the judgement calls that led to the choice of those definitions. The SysML model covers the actual processes, which are bound to the standards and literature they implement; the processes encoded become executable, so their properties become verifiable. The worked examples demonstrably conform to those processes and produce data that meets the specifications for the wires in the model. The formal properties can be checked (correct wiring, and any rule encoded as SHACL shape conformance), and the examples walk through to make it concrete and intuitive for a human reader. Each page of the MyST site is therefore a curated view of the underlying model. The updated outline delivers a story arc that uses the Popper bookends to make this intuitive for a general audience, then inside uses the formal engineering standards for contracting and for quality evaluation processes as a nested SysML model, rendered as RDF and enriched with the glossary content to ensure citation traceability; ultimately guaranteeing an auditable record of the AI evaluation done using OG-CAIE, by encoding and enforcing a DSO-conditioned EPO, and concluding that this record meets Popper's bar for being scientific. The task builds out what the model (representation) and the site (presentation) each must do. The separation of representation and presentation is one of the main value propositions of doing this with GitHub, MyST, Jupyter, Python, OpenSysML, rdflib, pySHACL and other executable systems engineering tools, which allow text-based standards to be codified in a formal record with machine-provable traceability in both directions and coverage. Eight pages, as listed; each page includes both the formal abstract specification and the relevant concrete example, the two running in parallel throughout, with a recognisable pattern so that the reader can find them. There is always more: highlighting the separation principle makes clear that the presentation layer (the site) is a view rather than the model itself (the repository). The presentation is calibrated for a human reader, so the texture and the volume of the content are tuned to human sensibilities. The representation layer is made further accessible to AI through CLI tools and skills, as was done for the glossary. In practice the views are tailored to carry the most important information for the human reader, and the concrete examples are made didactic relative to the abstract concepts; the two always appear as a pair.
nodes.label: R-34

nodes.desc: The walkthrough may describe two further steps that are explicitly not part of the contract lifecycle and are identified instead as observed in practice: the county health office tells the chatbot provider to implement changes that result in demonstrable behaviour change per the findings of Humane Intelligence, and the chatbot provider implements the changes, at which point the county health office may require new testing to certify that the flagged issues were addressed. This is not claimed to be in the contracting loop of the standard contracting process; it is an opportunity to show how the evaluation results in demonstrable system behaviour change. For safety-critical deployments these evaluations would be expected to be paired with a release. Since the sponsor organization and the chatbot provider are both already in the example, this is primarily narration, to help the reader understand what the process is like in practice and why it is not an academic exercise.
nodes.label: R-35

nodes.desc: The headword surveillance would raise eyebrows and is replaced. The citation to ISO/IEC 17000 8.1 surveillance stays mapped to the concept, since it is the formal doctrine on the subject, but an alternative headword is chosen, monitoring or oversight.
nodes.label: R-36

nodes.desc: An extra seam is added to account for any data covering the obligations, duties or expressed mission the sponsoring organization has with regard to the affected populations. This is context that informs what goes into the contract.
nodes.label: R-37

nodes.desc: Some connectivity should show how the mission of the sponsor organization relates to the affected population; it may be covered in the data but not in the view. Diagrams tend to be overloaded, so in practice they must stay simple, even if some wires are braided into bundles, since the information flows together in practice. Diagrams are important views for humans, so their density must be balanced against the point they make. As long as the code that produces a diagram reads from the model itself and the perspective the view encodes is documented (what it brings into focus and what it leaves out), any view that is compelling narratively is permitted. The view code is hardened by building reusable views and committing the methods with a CLI and skills for their use, which makes other views possible even though the presentation layer curates.
nodes.label: R-38

nodes.desc: A knowledge graph explorer is added as an appendix, modelled after the authors' earlier d3 work in several repositories. Since the text keeps saying there is more, it is easier to cut the text and link to the explorer. Given the extent of the OWL, SHACL and SPARQL work and the existing machine navigation tools, the human-facing graph exploration interface belongs in the appendix; it must back onto the RDF model (Oxigraph may be used for speed). The work may proceed in parallel with the main body. The appendix is an alternative user interface, not new content.
nodes.label: R-39

nodes.desc: In the example, one of the boundary items between the contract and the fulfilment of the evaluation contract covers the sponsor's decision that the commuters needed to be interviewed while the residents could simply be represented. This is the kind of judgement call that affects the scope of work: whether expert representation is accepted or interviews and documented stakeholder-needs input are required. The example case splits across two affected stakeholder groups to show that both options are valid and traceable under the EPO. In practice representation is the most common, with stakeholder interviews reserved for extenuating circumstances because of the increased level of effort, generally for under-represented stakeholders or under-documented stakeholder needs.
nodes.label: R-40

nodes.desc: The rulings move to an appendix. The concept is important, but most readers will not need it. The rulings are already part of the knowledge graph explorer; they fit best as Appendix C. The knowledge graph explorer allows navigation of the whole model and the computational proofs demonstrate the guarantees the model can prove computationally; Appendix C is the acknowledgement of the subjective choices, judgements and interpretations the model is grounded in. These subjectivities are implicit in the objective results the computational proofs produce, and the claim that this is scientific holds with these judgements as auxiliary assumptions. Appendix C is framed as the specification holding itself to its own definition of science.
nodes.label: R-41

nodes.desc: The page names are tightened: Glossary becomes Standards and Definitions; Contracting becomes Stakeholders and Contracting; The evaluation becomes Context and Evaluation; What the record proves becomes Records and Reporting; Conclusion stays. This gives a reader who skims the outline a much clearer picture of what the site contains. The appendices provide the first rung of backup and the repository as a whole an even richer one, so the reader need not take the authors on trust: the reader can verify.
nodes.label: R-42

nodes.desc: An Appendix D, Toolchain and Reproducibility, is added: a detailed review of the toolchain from virtual environments to the packages used, modelled after the portion of the SciPy proceedings supplementary material that covers the same subject. The reader should see that this is a computational paradigm, not just another document.
nodes.label: R-43

nodes.desc: The page title The nested model becomes A Nested Lifecycle: model is a throwaway word for most readers and should not trip anyone up. The nested lifecycle page must also address the fact that the records and reporting rely on information produced during both the contracting lifecycle and the evaluation lifecycle.
nodes.label: R-44

nodes.desc: OpenSysML is absent from the runtime environment because it was used only for modelling, through the features that render the models to RDF. The toolchain review therefore needs a section on ontologies, addressing PROV-O, EARL, SysML and the others.
nodes.label: R-45

nodes.desc: The layers diagram is illegible to a human and needs the treatment given to the earlier diagrams. Views are designed to communicate clearly as views, not to be exhaustive; this may require several diagrams, or it may be as simple as black-boxing subsystems more effectively. Wiring two systems together often means focusing on how they interface with each other, even when the interfaces span scales.
nodes.label: R-46

nodes.desc: Round one of the simulated user test is adjudicated item by item (sheet 06). The front page opens in three sentences and names the measles case early. The bridge cites the public Birds-of-a-Feather session at SciPy 2026 as a fact on the record rather than a private artefact; the forthcoming blog post may be added later. The chapters are reorganized: prose with headings that shape the outline, information blocks used sparingly, and code blocks that demonstrably pull content from the model, in the manner of the vendor fraud example. The rulings are rewritten in a formal register with their intent preserved and the message as sent kept in the graph. Terms are defined at first use, as the SciPy proceedings reviewers approved. The canonical source of outcome is SEVOCAB's test result; NIST TN 1297 is a reserve source; fragment quotes say so; Popper 1959 stands alongside every crosswalk row. The four weak step matches are re-cited from process canon, since the posture is implementation of standards and not their re-litigation, the contribution being the application to contextual AI evaluation and the executable specification. The coined terms cite nothing and are owned. ogc reads the record and exposes the executor's parameters. The thirteen pending quotes are ticked. Appendix D is aligned with the code it describes.
